unit_label: ABFM Module D unit 3 (courseware unit 21): private equity and venture capital

facts.statement: Venture capital (courseware): venture capital is a form of private equity and a type of finance supplied to new enterprises and start-ups that are believed to have the ability to grow rapidly; it may come as money or as specialised knowledge and managerial experience, and the investors expect a high rate of return. Venture capital exists because of deficiencies in bank lending: banks lend against tangible assets as collateral and many new businesses have few; the risk of a new venture is so high that interest rates high enough to compensate would be prohibitive; venture capitalists instead take a share of the company as compensation for the risk, so they participate in the upside; and venture capital includes strategic guidance as well as money. In India, risk capital was supplied before venture funds by development financial institutions; foreign investors later brought practices such as rigorous due diligence, a stringent track record test, active post-investment involvement and attention to timely exit.

Characteristics of venture capital investments (courseware): the investor takes a high level of risk in the hope of a high return; the venture capitalist provides funding and also takes an active interest in leading the company; the investment is often by subscription to stock or quasi-equity instruments, so the investor shares both risk and profit; the financial burden on the aided company is often minimal in the early years; and the venture capitalist normally has an exit strategy within about three to seven years, often with the promoter having the first option to buy back the equity held by the venture capital fund.

Private equity and venture capital compared (courseware): shared characteristics are that both are autonomous pools of capital with contributions from institutions or high-net-worth individuals and managers with strong financial incentives tied to the fund returns; both invest in businesses that cannot or are not ready to raise money from the public; there are few restrictions on their activities; and both oversee investee companies actively under carefully drafted agreements. Distinctions: a private equity investment might be used to restructure the finances or operations of the investee; private equity typically goes into established, later-stage businesses with a proven track record, whereas venture capital backs earlier stages; private equity places a greater premium on good corporate governance while venture capital emphasises management capability; and a private equity deal may include debt, which is unusual in venture capital.

Stages of venture capital financing (courseware): the three broad forms are financing for the initial stages of development, financing for expansion, and acquisition financing. By stage of the business: low-level finance to validate and develop an idea (seed); financing for new businesses in formative stages for product development and marketing; initial investment to fund manufacturing and early sales; a second round of financing, an operational capital injection, for early-stage firms that are selling but not yet profitable; a third round, mezzanine financing, to expand after early success; and a fourth round, bridge financing, to prepare for going public.

Procedure for venture capital funding (courseware): six steps. (1) Beginning of a transaction: a business relationship is established and deals usually originate through referrals from business partners, parent organisations, friends and contacts. (2) Screening and shortlisting: ventures are sorted by criteria such as technology or product, size of investment, geography and stage of financing; entrepreneurs give a concise profile or meet face to face. (3) Detailed evaluation and rating: the project is given a rating, and the review covers the project and the entrepreneur (experience, technical competence, manufacturing and marketing ability, entrepreneurial talent). (4) Final deal negotiations: the amount invested, the percentage of profit held by each party and the rights of each party are negotiated to make the deal win-win. (5) Post-investment activities: the venture capitalist joins as investor, is normally represented on the board of directors, and does not run day-to-day operations. (6) Exit plan: designed to produce the greatest gain with the fewest losses, through an initial public offering, acquisition by another business, or purchase by the promoter or an outsider.

Advantages and drawbacks of venture capital (courseware): advantages are a large amount of wealth and expertise, a large funding capacity through equity, and no obligation on the business owner to repay if the venture fails because the investor understands the risk. Drawbacks are a drawn-out and difficult procedure with significant risk, the founder losing some independence and control once the investor becomes a part owner, delayed returns from the long-term nature of the investment, and uncertainty about the use and return on the investment. For new businesses, venture capital is often preferred to a stock market listing, which has many conditions, and to loans, which put pressure on a young business that is not yet profitable to pay interest; venture capitalists usually invest for about five years and then sell their stake, for example when the company needs more capital and sells shares or lists through an initial public offering.

Roles at a venture capital firm (courseware): analysts (junior staff who attend conferences, research markets and look for opportunities within the fund thesis); associates (junior or senior; build relationships and make a first impression on decision makers but do not take part in the decision); principals (on the edge of becoming partners, with authority but not among the most senior); partners (general partners or managing partners, who make investment decisions and bring in new financial backing, and are not involved in day-to-day operations of investee companies; their compensation includes carry); entrepreneur in residence (EIR; an experienced entrepreneur working with the firm for about a year or a year and a half to help find business opportunities); and limited partners (LPs; individuals or institutions that invest in the funds managed by the firm, such as endowments, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, funds of funds and wealthy families). General partners raise capital from LPs, invest (deal flow, due diligence and writing the cheque), help investee companies grow (strategy, recruitment, introductions) and exit (initial public offering, merger or acquisition, or a secondary sale), after which proceeds are distributed to LPs.

Terms of venture capital funding (courseware): a fund has a size, a theme (industry, stage and region), a hurdle rate (the minimum annual return, measured as an internal rate of return, that the manager is required to deliver to limited partners; it depends on the sector and stage, so a seed-stage fund has a higher hurdle than a later-stage one) and a fund life of seven to ten years, divided roughly into two to three years of finding and investing, three to four years of building the businesses and a final two to three years of exiting. Deal structure: preferred equity (ranking ahead of common stock in a sale or closure, taking the assets and technology before common holders), voting rights clauses on major decisions such as listing or sale, and anti-dilution clauses that adjust the number of shares if a later round is at a lower value so that the fund keeps the same percentage. Fees: a management fee of about two to three per cent of fund size a year, covering the manager time, rent, salaries and costs; and carry (carried interest), a bonus on the fund profit, with limited partners receiving about 70 to 80 per cent of profit and general partners about 20 to 30 per cent, so that managers are motivated to maximise returns. The venture capital firm often runs several funds, each with its own life, focus and minimum investment.

Returns, failure and the power law (courseware): venture capital is expected to earn more than public equity and debt, and a fund targeting an annualised return needs its assets to grow by a multiple of the original size over its life. The success of a company needs many things to go right (sufficient capital, capable management, product development, sourcing, competitor behaviour, customer demand, pricing, patents); even if each has an 80 per cent chance, eight such events together give only about 17 per cent, and lowering one of them to 50 per cent gives about 10 per cent, so many backed businesses fail. Venture returns follow a power law: not every investment must be profitable, because one or two big winners can make up for the losses of the rest; investors therefore look for businesses in very large markets with very fast growth, asking whether an investment could expand many times in four to five years; most funds do not produce high returns and some return less than the money invested.

Value venture capitalists contribute and how they select (courseware): entrepreneurs should consider a venture capitalist for strategy, introductions, access to a network of other entrepreneurs and infrastructure such as specialist staff, marketers and recruiters, not only for the money. Founders are advised to ask about the track record, how the firm works with portfolio companies, whether it has recently made investments (a gap of many months may mean difficulty raising its next fund), the option pool allocation and how long fund raising takes. The selection process is a funnel: of thousands of deals sourced each year only a very small fraction (under one per cent) is funded; stages are sourcing, deal screen, partners review, due diligence, investment committee and deployment.

Private equity (courseware): private equity is non-publicly traded capital in the alternative investments class; funds and investors invest directly in private companies or buy out public companies, which can end in delisting. Funding comes from institutional and individual investors and is used for new technologies, acquisitions, working capital and strengthening balance sheets. Structure: the private equity firm is the general partner, the investors are limited partners (public and corporate pension funds, insurance companies, high-net-worth individuals, family offices, endowments, foundations, funds of funds, sovereign wealth funds) and the fund is a limited partnership; limited partners normally own 99 per cent of the fund and have limited liability while the general partner owns 1 per cent with full liability. Benefits: an alternative to bank loans (high interest, covenants) or listing; reduced pressure of quarterly results; more patient capital for turnarounds. Drawbacks: holdings are hard to liquidate because there is no ready market; prices are set by negotiation, not the market; shareholder rights are decided case by case, not by a broad governance framework. Sources of funds are mostly institutional investors and accredited individuals with long commitments; liquidity comes through an initial public offering or a sale.

Forms of private equity and how firms earn (courseware): funding in difficult times (distress investing: buy troubled businesses to sell their assets at a profit or turn them around); leveraged buyouts (buy a company mostly with debt, improve it and resell or list it; an acquisition vehicle, often a special purpose vehicle, is used, and up to about 90 per cent of the funds may come from debt); real estate private equity (including real estate investment trusts); fund of funds (invest in other funds, giving access to investors who cannot meet minimums, at the cost of a second layer of fees); and venture capital (seed financing to build a concept into a product, Series A to enter an existing industry or build a new one, and early-stage finance to grow). Revenue of a private equity firm comes mainly from management fees (a percentage of assets under management, often two per cent) and performance fees (often 20 per cent of profit on the sale of an investment); there is much competition for jobs because of the large fees. Courseware criticism: the high incomes of private equity staff led to calls for transparency.

Legal and administrative structure in India (courseware): private equity funds are typically organised as trusts and registered with SEBI as alternative investment funds (AIFs) under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012, which replaced the earlier venture capital fund regulations; they can also be set up as companies or limited liability partnerships. An AIF is a privately pooled investment vehicle that collects funds from sophisticated investors, Indian or foreign, for investing under a defined policy. Category I AIFs invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs or infrastructure or sectors the government or regulators consider socially or economically desirable (venture capital funds, SME funds, social venture funds, infrastructure funds, angel funds). Category II AIFs do not fall in categories I or III and do not use leverage other than to meet day-to-day operating needs (private equity funds, debt funds, funds for distressed assets, real estate funds). Category III AIFs use diverse or complex trading strategies and may use leverage, including through investment in listed or unlisted derivatives (hedge funds, PIPE funds). A private equity fund primarily invests in equity or equity-linked instruments of investee companies. An angel fund is a sub-category of venture capital fund under Category I that raises funds from angel investors by issue of units; the courseware gives eligibility and size conditions which are not taught. The Companies Act restricts private companies from offering securities to the general public, so they raise capital by private placement to a limited number of persons; because private equity funds do not raise money from the public, regulation of investments in them is lighter. SEBI issues circulars on reporting, disclosure, overseas investment and compliance.

Process of investing in private equity (courseware): in India most private equity investment is in privately held companies; types include seed capital, angel investment, venture capital, growth capital and late-stage investment, buyouts and turnaround capital. A typical transaction has these steps: (1) a teaser sent by investment bankers (a condensed, anonymous summary of the opportunity); (2) a non-disclosure agreement; (3) a confidential information memorandum; (4) valuation by the bidder from financial data and projections; (5) an expression of interest (a non-binding offer indicating a price); (6) access to data for due diligence; (7) management meetings; (8) a letter of intent outlining broad conditions; and (9) the contract for purchase of shares or assets, which is binding. Due diligence is the investigation of the target covering commercial and legal matters in addition to accounting and tax; it protects the buyer from dangers and flaws, and helps the seller by showing the real value. The overview covers financial matters, corporate matters, customer relationships and sales, contractual matters, employee issues, litigation, tax, intellectual property and related party transactions.

Exit strategies for private equity (courseware): a private equity fund is typically planned with a life of five to ten years, and the investor starts planning the exit right after purchase. Strategies: initial public offering (listing the shares; the exit is complete only when the shares are sold); trade sale (selling all shares to a third-party buyer such as a competitor, with cash realised almost immediately); secondary buyout (selling the investment to another private equity fund, giving a clean exit); the procedure with two separate tracks (preparing both an initial public offering and a sale at once and choosing the better); and recapitalisation through leverage (raising debt to be the majority of capitalisation to pay a large dividend or buy back shares, a partial exit that also increases the risk of failure).

payload.title: Venture capital and why it exists
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Venture capital (VC)** is a form of **private equity** supplied to **new enterprises and start-ups** that may **grow rapidly**. It brings **money and know-how**, and the investors expect a **high return**.

**Why it exists** (gaps in bank lending):

- Banks lend against **tangible collateral**; new businesses have **few assets**.
- The **risk is so high** that a lending rate high enough to compensate would be **prohibitive**.
- A VC takes a **share of the company** instead and so **shares the upside**.
- A VC adds **strategic guidance**, not only funds.

In India, **development financial institutions** supplied risk capital first; **foreign investors** later brought **rigorous due diligence, track-record tests, active post-investment involvement and a focus on timely exit**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The investor accepts equity-style risk because a loan would price the risk out of reach.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do banks seldom finance a brand-new venture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The venture has little collateral and its risk is too high to price in an interest rate.

payload.title: Characteristics of venture capital investments
payload.core_explanation_md:
1. The investor takes a **high level of risk** for a **high return**.
2. The VC gives **funding** and also takes an **active interest in leading** the company.
3. The investment is often by **subscription to stock or quasi-equity instruments**, so the VC **shares risk and profit**.
4. The **financial burden on the company is minimal in the early years**.
5. The VC has an **exit strategy**, normally in **three to seven years**, often with the **promoter having the first option** to buy back the VC equity.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The low early burden fits a business with no profit yet.

self_check.prompt_text: Within about how many years does a VC normally plan an exit?

payload.title: Private equity and venture capital: similarities and differences
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Shared:** **autonomous pools of capital** funded by **institutions and high-net-worth investors**; managers with **strong financial incentives**; investees that **cannot or are not ready** to raise money from the public; **few restrictions** on activities; **active oversight** under **carefully drafted agreements**.

| Private equity (PE) | Venture capital (VC) |
| --- | --- |
| **Established, later-stage** businesses with a **track record** | **Earlier stages** |
| May be used to **restructure finances or operations** | Funds **growth** |
| Greater premium on **corporate governance** | Greater attention to **management capability** |
| A deal **may include debt** | Debt is **unusual** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Venture capital is a sub-type of private equity focused on young high-growth firms.

self_check.prompt_text: In which type of investment is debt usually part of the deal?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Private equity; it is unusual in venture capital.

payload.title: Terms of a venture fund: size, theme, hurdle, life and deal structure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Fund size and theme:** the **amount** to be raised and the **industry, stage and region**.

**Hurdle rate:** the **minimum annual return (IRR)** the manager must deliver to LPs; it depends on **sector and stage** (a **seed** fund has a **higher** hurdle than a later-stage fund).

**Fund life: 7 to 10 years**: about **2 to 3 years** investing, **3 to 4** building the businesses, **2 to 3** exiting.

**Deal structure:** **preferred equity** (ranks **ahead of common** in a sale or closure), **voting rights clauses** on major decisions (listing, sale) and **anti-dilution clauses** (if a later round is at a **lower value**, the share count is adjusted so the fund keeps its **percentage**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Preferred equity protects the fund when a venture is sold for less than hoped.

self_check.prompt_text: What does an anti-dilution clause protect?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The fund percentage ownership if a later round is priced lower.

payload.title: Fees, carry and fund economics
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Management fee** = **fee rate x fund size** each year; courseware indication: about **2 to 3 per cent** of fund size, covering the manager time and running costs.

**Carry (carried interest)** = **carry rate x fund profit**; courseware indication: **limited partners about 70 to 80 per cent** and **general partners about 20 to 30 per cent** of profits.

**LP profit = (1 - carry rate) x profit.**

PE funds: **limited partners about 99 per cent** of the fund with limited liability, **general partner about 1 per cent** with full liability (courseware indication).

Typical terms **vary by fund**.

variables.name: Profit of the fund after returning invested capital

assumptions: Profit is shared on the agreed split
Terms are those of the particular fund
common_errors: Applying carry to the whole fund instead of the profit
Taking the management fee on the profit

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Carry rewards the manager only if the fund makes money, aligning interests with the LPs.

self_check.prompt_text: On what base is the management fee charged?
self_check.expected_takeaway: On the fund size, each year.

payload.title: Returns: multiples, annual growth, probability and the power law
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Multiple of invested capital = value returned / amount invested.**

**Annual growth needed to reach a multiple M in n years: (M^(1/n) - 1).** Ten times in ten years needs about **25.9 per cent** a year (the courseware rounds to 25 per cent).

**Probability of overall success = product of the probabilities of each needed event.** Eight events at **80 per cent** each give **0.8^8, about 17 per cent**; if one falls to **50 per cent** the result is about **10 per cent**. So **many backed businesses fail**.

**Power law:** a **few big winners** can pay for the **many losses**, so VCs pursue **very large markets** with **very fast growth**.

common_errors: Dividing the multiple by the years
Adding the probabilities instead of multiplying

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A single outsized winner can return the whole fund even if most investments fail.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the power law say about venture returns?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A few very large successes can make up for the losses on the rest.

payload.title: Legal structure of private equity and venture funds in India

An **AIF** is a **privately pooled vehicle** collecting funds from **sophisticated investors**, Indian or foreign, under a **defined investment policy**.

| Category | Invests in | Examples | Leverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **I** | **Start-ups, early-stage, social ventures, SMEs, infrastructure** (socially or economically desirable) | **VC, SME, social venture, infrastructure, angel funds** | n/a |

payload.title: Exit strategies of private equity funds
payload.core_explanation_md:
A PE fund has a **planned life of about five to ten years**; the investor plans the **exit right after buying**.

| --- | --- |
| **Initial public offering** | **Listing the shares**; the exit is complete **only when the shares are sold** |

The category descriptions are taught at the level of principle; all figures, thresholds and counts are held back because the AIF regulations have been amended since and no primary source was retrieved.

The courseware narrates many deals, firms, statistics and forecasts (KKR and JBF, Pepperfry, Indian venture firms and their portfolios, the list of international and Indian private equity firms and their ticket sizes, India market size and growth, 2021 and 2022 fundraising, the seven near-future trends and SPAC commentary, mutual fund and REIT amounts, historic leveraged buyouts such as Carnegie Steel and RJR Nabisco). These are dated narrative, were not checked and are not taught or tested.

The courseware states that a fund needing to earn 25 per cent a year must grow its assets ten times over ten years. Ten times over ten years is a compound growth of about 25.9 per cent, and 25 per cent a year gives about 9.3 times; the courseware figure is an approximation. The calculation items use the exact formula.

The courseware states typical fee terms (management fee of about 2 to 3 per cent of fund size a year; carry of 20 to 30 per cent of profit, with limited partners receiving 70 to 80 per cent; limited partners owning 99 per cent and general partners 1 per cent; fund life of 7 to 10 years; return of 25 to 35 per cent for venture against 12 to 15 per cent for equity and 8 to 10 per cent for debt). These are presented as courseware indications of typical terms, which vary by fund, and are used only in items framed that way.

The portfolio return item uses new numbers.

The liquidation preference arithmetic (preferred holders paid first up to the amount invested) and the hurdle compounding item are standard finance applied to the courseware statements that preferred equity ranks ahead of common on a sale and that the hurdle rate is the minimum annual return; the courseware gives no worked terms.
